Roy Takano leads a town hall meeting, Manzanar Relocation Center, California. By Ansel Adams. 1943.

Ansel Adams, most renowned for his landscape photography, was invited by the Warden of this WWII Japanese-American relocation camp to document the living conditions and daily lives of the "inhabitants". "The purpose of my work was to show how these people, suffering under a great injustice, and loss of property, businesses and professions, had overcome the sense of defeat and despair by building for themselves a vital community in an arid (but magnificent) environment," he said.

Many more of his photographs of the Camp may be found here.

Of the 110,000 Japanese-Americans who were forced to live in internment camps, about 10,000 were housed at Manzanar, the largest Center. The camp was designed to be largely self-managed and self-sufficient and internees were employed raising crops, tending to the orchards, raising and slaughtering hogs and chickens, etc. Various other services were established such as schools, a newspaper, beauty and barber shops, shoe repair, sports facilities and more.

In 1985, Manzanar was designated a National Historic Landmark.
